newsitem.title: USA: US crude outlook - demand fanned by heat oil, storm.
newsitem.headline: US crude outlook - demand fanned by heat oil, storm.

text.p: U.S. crude prices are likely to stay stubbornly resistant to its own fundamentals, leaning on bullish heating oil and a revival in heat-to-crude cracks for upward momentum, traders and analysts said Monday.
The threat to crude deliveries in the Gulf Coast, as Tropical Storm Josephine swirls on the doorstep of the U.S. largest refining region, also kept the price ascent intact.
"Prices will continue higher. The push from the storm comes on the heels of a nervous market, which means setbacks will be regained," a trader in Washington, D.C., said.
Recent chills in the U.S northeast and low inventories were deemed a potent brew for West Texas Intermediate to take another stab at $25.70 a barrel, its post-Gulf War high.
NYMEX November spot crude reached an early Monday high of $25.23 a barrel, and some traders and analysts predicted an assault at $26 in the very near future.
"The market's going at a good clip. The heat cracks have been so strong, there should be continued high runs in the 90's," the Washington, D.C. trader said.
U.S. refinery runs have been going full throttle at 95.5 percent for the last week of September.
With heating oil up six cents a gallon since October 1, refiners have raced to capitalize on returns.
"Basically, the sky's the limit," said Tom Bentz, energy analyst at ING Derivatives in New York. "It's low stocks, cold weather, and it's technical strength," Bentz said.
Crude oil imports have been restricted by poor arbitrage economics lately, reducing North Sea Brent price-related crude cargoes from Europe and West Africa.
Domestic crudes are already benefitting, with Louisiana grades gaining another five cents since late Friday and seen spiralling higher if there should be loss if U.S. Gulf output.
Tropical Storm Josephine is currently located 340 miles southwest of Apalachicola, Fla. and has maximum winds of near 50 miles per hour.
The Louisiana Offshore Oil Port (LOOP) shut since Saturday is estimated to reopen midweek, but some oil production in the U.S. Gulf has been shut-in ahead of the storm.
The delay of some four to five crude tankers waiting to deliver at the LOOP, also gave domestic crudes support.
Separately, last week's government approval of further sour crude sales from the U.S. Stragetic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) pressured domestic heavy grades only moderately.
"The SPR volumes will dribble into the market," one trader said, but added that for the present price spike, it would be "too little, too late, to help at that point."
